title: Rabbi Levi bar Chayta
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: English translation and editorial notes prepared for Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: In Moed Katan 29a, he said: “Someone taking leave of the dead should not say, ‘Go to peace,’ but ‘Go in peace.’ Someone taking leave of the living should say, ‘Go to peace,’ as it is written,” etc. Afterward it says: “And Rabbi Levi said”—“bar Chita,” according to a manuscript cited in Dikdukei Soferim—“Anyone who leaves the synagogue for the study hall merits receiving the Divine Presence, as it is written,” etc.[^1]

In Yerushalmi Shabbat, at the end of chapter 6, Rabbi Levi bar Chayuta said, concerning the words of Rabbi Berekhya in the name of Rabbi Abba bar Kahana: “Has He not already done so in this world? This is what is written,” etc. In Yerushalmi Sotah 7:1, Rabbi Levi bar Chita went to Caesarea and heard people reciting the Shema in Greek. He wished to stop them; Rabbi Yosi heard and became angry. The statement is cited under the dictionary entry Aleksnin, where the name is Rabbi Levi bar Chorta.[^2]
In Bereishit Rabbah 55:5, Rabbi Levi bar Chayta said: “Twice it is written, ‘Go forth,’” etc.[^3]
In Bereishit Rabbah 39:11, Rabbi Levi bar Chavyat and Rabbi Abba, the son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, said, etc. Perhaps the name should read bar Chavit or Chayta.[^4]

notes.text: The contrast is between le-shalom, “to peace,” for the living, and be-shalom, “in peace,” for the dead. Hyman’s bracket supplies the patronymic bar Chita in the second saying from Dikdukei Soferim’s manuscript evidence.

The Greek-language term is printed אלוניסתין, which Hyman glosses “in Greek”; the dictionary headword he cites is אלכסנין. The patronymics in these passages vary: חיותא (Chayuta), חיתה (Chita) and חורתא (Chorta).
Lekh lekha, “Go forth,” is the wording of God’s commands to Abraham in Genesis 12:1 and 22:2.
The last citation reads חויית (Chavyat). Hyman proposes חוית (Chavit) or חייתא (Chayta), retaining the identification as a possibility.
